title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We report a preregistered paired trial that measures whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single shared LLM generation per intent, deterministic verification, and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted verifier‑unsafe network changes relative to LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. Following preregistration (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N = 500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles using gpt-5-mini for generation and a deterministic network verifier for adjudication. Observed accepted final changes: baseline (LLM-only) 496/500; guarded (GVR) 500/500. Paired contingency: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The preregistered exact conditional two‑sided McNemar test on the discordant margin (n = 4, k = n10 = 4) yields p = 0.125. A predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates (one repair attempt per repaired task); total hosted model calls observed = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls), mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and bootstrap perspectives, document verifier semantics and known blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting semantics, present representative repaired‑episode diagnostics, and point readers to the archived evidence bundle and preregistration for full machine‑readable artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation from high‑level operator intent to device configuration promises material productivity gains for network operations, but generated CLI sequences that violate workflow or availability constraints can produce outages. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied for intent translation and AIOps, yet hallucination and factual errors remain primary reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A pragmatic architectural mitigation is generate–verify–repair (GVR): have an LLM produce a single shared candidate canonical CLI sequence, deterministically verify that candidate against explicit workflow, dependency, and availability rules, and when the verifier finds violations invoke a constrained, bounded repair attempt. GVR preserves a low‑latency single initial generation while using deterministic rules to adjudicate safety before acceptance.

This paper reports a preregistered controlled paired experiment that asks: does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → at most one automated repair) produce fewer accepted verifier‑unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? We executed the preregistered protocol (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) on N = 500 paired intents (1000 total condition episodes) using a single declared generation model (gpt-5-mini) and a domain‑specific deterministic verifier. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired trial executed end‑to‑end with frozen seeds and archived artifacts that report exact execution counts and diagnostic traces; (2) a detailed, evidence‑grounded description of generation semantics, deterministic verifier capabilities, and the bounded repair loop used as the GVR gate; and (3) reconciled inferential reporting that follows the preregistered exact conditional McNemar decision rule while also presenting the predeclared exploratory bootstrap interval and per‑episode verifier diagnostics for the repaired cases. All numerical results, accounting, and per‑episode diagnostics reported here are taken verbatim from the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work:
This study synthesizes three strands of prior work that motivated our design. First, surveys and system papers document active interest in LLMs for intent translation, NetOps automation, and multi‑agent orchestration while repeatedly highlighting hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers; these motivate adding deterministic validation gates to generation pipelines [doi:10.1145/3718958.3750537; https://openalex.org/W4411735779; doi:10.1002/nem.2313]. Second, methodological proposals for evaluate‑and‑repair architectures emphasize standardized validator semantics, paired trial designs, frozen preregistration, and accounting for orchestration costs (model calls, repair attempts) when assessing safety improvements; those blueprints informed our preregistered estimand and confirmatory test choice (exact conditional McNemar) and our provider‑call accounting requirements [https://openalex.org/W4403443637]. Third, deterministic and scalable network configuration verifiers have matured to check syntactic, workflow, dependency, and many availability properties at scale; such verifiers can detect sequencing and paired‑field hazards but their scope depends on modeled vendor and control‑plane semantics [https://openalex.org/W4413757123].

Across these literatures the common theme is that tool‑augmented LLM pipelines—LLMs coupled to deterministic checkers, simulators, or specialized parsers—reduce a subset of unsafe outputs, but the effectiveness and operational sufficiency depend critically on verifier fidelity, the nature of task artifacts, and how detection costs scale. Our experiment positions itself as a reproducible, controlled evaluation of a minimal GVR gate using a canonical deterministic verifier rather than as a broad production claim across diverse vendor environments.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration, estimand, and design: The study was preregistered (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 distinct intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). Sampling seeds and the deterministic task generator were frozen prior to execution. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar on discordant pairs; a predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was declared for descriptive interval estimation.

Task generation and intent grammar: Intents were synthesized by a deterministic task generator that emits a task manifest entry per intent. Each manifest contains an initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_touched_fields, workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, make_before_break patterns), and a required_sequence that represents the canonical safe command ordering. Tasks vary in difficulty (patterns such as shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) and are stratified by topology profile to exercise availability and dependency constraints in the verifier.

Generation semantics, orchestration, and repair policy: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model gpt-5-mini with fixed generation configuration. Under the baseline condition the shared candidate was accepted without verifier‑driven repair. Under the guarded (GVR) condition the controller validated the shared candidate and, if verification failed, invoked at most one automated repair attempt using the same model and a constrained repair template that included (a) the original intent abstraction, (b) the verifier violation codes and short descriptions, and (c) an explicit request to return a corrected canonical CLI sequence. Repairs were accepted only if the verifier returned valid = true. Provider accounting recorded model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls); stage_counts recorded shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4. Mean hosted model calls per accepted change = 504/500 = 1.008. For repaired pairs the observed model calls per pair = 2 (shared initial + one repair).

Deterministic verifier semantics and scoring: The adjudicating verifier canonicalizes and parses the normalized CLI sequence and then applies a deterministic rule set. The pipeline performs: (i) syntactic parsing and canonical normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison with the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome. For each episode the verifier emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, a violation list and codes, and a boolean valid. The scorer used for primary outcomes is the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with scoring_rule full_intent_constraint_validation. A human‑readable codebook maps violation codes to descriptions; per‑episode verifier traces and diagnostics were archived for the repaired episodes and for auditing.

Statistical analysis plan (preregistered): Each paired intent yields two binary outcomes (final accepted change passes verifier? true/false). The primary confirmatory test conditions on the observed discordant margin and uses the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar (binomial tail) on k = n10 with p = 0.5. Secondary and exploratory outputs include the predeclared paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples and seed = 1729. The preregistration specified Bonferroni multiplicity for two confirmatory tests, but the templated‑automation arm was not executed and thus multiplicity adjustment across two confirmatory tests was not applied to these reported results.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and raw counts: Execution completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 1000; completed_pair_count = 500) with no failed episodes. Observed accepted‑change counts were baseline 496/500 (0.992) and guarded 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency table was n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked in four episodes; each repair attempt produced a subsequent verifier PASS. Provider accounting: model_calls_used = 504 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 4).

Primary confirmatory analysis (preregistered): The exact conditional McNemar conditions on the observed discordant margin n = n10 + n01 = 4 and evaluates a two‑sided binomial tail on k = n10 = 4 with p = 0.5. For n = 4 and k = 4 the one‑sided tail P(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16; doubling for two‑sided yields p = 0.125. Under the preregistered decision rule this p‑value does not meet the confirmatory threshold and we therefore do not claim confirmatory statistical significance.

Exploratory interval estimate (predeclared): The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference was computed with 10,000 resamples and seed = 1729 and equals [0.002, 0.016]. The bootstrap resampling did not condition on the observed discordant margin and thus can exclude zero when repeated resamples include the few favorable discordant outcomes; small discordant counts reduce frequentist coverage guarantees for percentile intervals and the bootstrap CI is therefore reported descriptively as predeclared.

Repaired‑episode diagnostics (artifact‑grounded summaries): The four repaired/discordant pairs corresponded to verifier‑detectable sequencing or group/paired‑field dependency violations. The archived per‑pair verifier violation codes and short descriptions are reported here exactly as recorded in the validator traces:

- pair-000090 | violation_codes: [MUST_BE_DOWN_FOR_FIELD] — "VLAN/field changed while interface remained admin up; required 'must be down' sequencing violated." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000341 | violation_codes: [MAKE_BEFORE_BREAK] — "Backup uplink not enabled before primary was shut; violates 'make‑before‑break' availability rule." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000381 | violation_codes: [PAIRED_MTU_CHANGE] — "MTU changed on one side of a paired link without coordinating the paired interface's MTU change (paired‑field dependency)." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.
- pair-000413 | violation_codes: [GROUP_AVAILABILITY_CONSTRAINT] — "Both edge interfaces placed admin down simultaneously, violating minimum_active_in_groups availability constraint." | repair_invoked: yes | model_calls_used_for_pair: 2 | final_score: PASS.

Representative per‑episode verifier diagnostics, normalized configurations, violation lists, parsed and required command counts, and the repair prompt/response transcripts for the repaired episodes are archived in the evidence bundle. The numerical totals, contingency counts, bootstrap parameters (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729), and p‑value reported above are taken directly from the archived analysis results.
sections.discussion:
Reconciling McNemar and bootstrap perspectives: The GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted; these correspond to the four discordant pairs (n = 4, k = 4). The preregistered exact conditional McNemar test conditions on the observed discordant margin and yields two‑sided p = 0.125, which does not meet the preregistered confirmatory threshold. The predeclared exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero ([0.002, 0.016]) because the bootstrap resampling scheme does not condition on margins and frequently resamples the same small set of favorable discordant outcomes. Both results are informative: McNemar enforces the preregistered decision rule and is conservative under small discordant counts; the bootstrap interval provides an additional descriptive estimate of magnitude but requires caution due to small‑discordant count coverage limitations. We therefore adhere to the preregistered McNemar rule for the primary claim while reporting the bootstrap interval as predeclared exploratory evidence.

Verifier scope, blind spots, and operational sufficiency: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. These checks are necessary to detect many syntactic and workflow errors that LLMs commonly produce within our intent grammar and were sufficient to flag the four repaired episodes in this run. The verifier intentionally omits vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing and convergence effects, session/execution‑time errors, hardware resource limits, and subtle environment side effects; therefore a verifier PASS is necessary for experiment safety but not sufficient to guarantee production safety. Operational automation would require expanded verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, timing/convergence models) and live telemetry‑driven validation prior to unsupervised execution.

Operational implications and cost tradeoffs: Under the bounded repair policy observed here (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) the repair invocation rate was 4/500 (0.8%) producing modest additional model calls: hosted model_call events = 504 (500 shared initial + 4 repairs). In contexts with low baseline failure rates this low overhead suggests that a compact deterministic verifier acting as a low‑latency gate can materially reduce verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals at modest model‑call cost. Quantities that determine operational cost and feasibility—verifier runtime at inventory scale, how repair frequency scales under adversarial or more diverse intents, and latency tradeoffs when using higher‑fidelity verifiers—remain important engineering considerations.

Threats to validity and generality: Internal validity is supported by preregistration, frozen seeds, deterministic task generation, and complete execution accounting (complete_pair_count = 500; failed_episode_count = 0). Construct validity is limited by the verifier abstraction level and synthetic device templates; the verifier enforces encoded workflow and group constraints that match the synthetic intent grammar, but these rules imperfectly model vendor behavior and dynamic control‑plane hazards. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication, vendor‑specific parsing, and live telemetry tests are required to generalize. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08; the observed near‑ceiling baseline (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs and reduced realized power relative to the preregistered assumption. Collectively these limitations explain why a modest numerical paired difference appears in the exploratory bootstrap interval but not in the preregistered exact McNemar decision.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 produces an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016] while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification combined with a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in the studied synthetic setting; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated‑automation comparator which was not executed in this run. Archival artifacts including the preregistration, model configuration, raw results, per‑episode verifier traces, provider accounting, and analysis logs are available in the evidence bundle for independent verification and audit as documented in the preregistration record.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. The generation model used in the archived run was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration). Key automated components in the run were a deterministic task generator, a deterministic network verifier, and a GVR controller implementing shared_initial_generation plus at most one automated repair per task. The study was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here are: N = 500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The immutable initial master prompt for this run is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt) and its SHA‑256 is 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and this revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this archived run; therefore the original preregistered multiplicity plan that would have adjusted for two confirmatory tests was not applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to the deterministic verifier’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan was not applied and the familywise error interpretation across two planned tests is not applicable to the present execution.
